title: Behind "Demon Castle 24-Hour Guard Shift" — Nurse Scheduling (NSP) and Linearization
contentHtml:
Mathematical Optimization (MILP) Formulation Guide MILP

Behind "Demon Castle 24-Hour Guard Shift":
Nurse Scheduling (NSP) and Linearization of Logical Rules

TL;DR — This article explains how real-world staff rostering and nurse scheduling models map directly onto the game's mechanics: rest intervals after night shifts, consecutive work limits, rookie supervision rules, and McCormick linearization of pairwise synergies and conflicts.

01Guard Shift Puzzle and the Nurse Scheduling Problem (NSP)

One of the most widely deployed applications of Operations Research (OR) is the Nurse Scheduling Problem (NSP) or Staff Rostering. "Demon Castle 24-Hour Guard Shift" adapts this practical MILP formulation into a fantasy castle defense puzzle.

Game Element Real-World Shift Scheduling Counterpart Mathematical Model Representation
Guard Monster m ∈ M Staff member, nurse, security guard Index set M (each with skill levels and stamina caps)
Day d ∈ D and Shift s ∈ {day, night} Planning horizon days and shift slots Binary decision variables x_{m,d,day}, x_{m,d,night} ∈ {0, 1}
Hero Army Raid Power R_{d,s} Required skill coverage / forecasted demand per slot Right-hand side constant of the Covering Constraint
No Day Shift After a Night Shift Minimum rest interval between shifts Pairwise exclusion x_{m,d,night} + x_{m,d+1,day} <= 1
Consecutive / Weekly Caps & Days Off Labor regulations, weekly caps, requested PTO Sliding-window constraints and variable fixing
Pururu's "No Solo Night Shift" Junior staff supervision (no solo night duty) Logical implication constraint
Synergy Pairs (+100) & Clashes (-150) Preferred pairing / incompatible staff avoidance McCormick linearization variable p_{A,B,d,s} for x_A * x_B

02Decision Variables and Labor Rule Formulation

Let $D = \{0, 1, \dots, T-1\}$ denote the planning days and $M$ denote the on-duty guard roster. For each guard $m \in M$ and day $d \in D$, we define binary variables $\text{day}_{m,d} \in \{0, 1\}$ and $\text{night}_{m,d} \in \{0, 1\}$ (if both are $0$, guard $m$ rests on day $d$).

Labor & Rest Interval Constraints (for all m ∈ M) $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{(1) At most 1 shift per day:} && \text{day}_{m,d} + \text{night}_{m,d} \le 1 && (\forall d \in D) \\ &\text{(2) No Night}\to\text{Next Day:} && \text{night}_{m,d} + \text{day}_{m,d+1} \le 1 && (\forall d \in \{0, \dots, T-2\}) \\ &\text{(3) Weekly shift cap:} && \sum_{d \in D} (\text{day}_{m,d} + \text{night}_{m,d}) \le W_m \\ &\text{(4) Requested day off (PTO):} && \text{day}_{m,d} + \text{night}_{m,d} = 0 && (\forall (m, d) \in \text{OffRequests}) \end{aligned} $$

Maximum Consecutive Working Days (Sliding-Window Formulation)

To enforce rules such as "Elder Dragon Drago can work at most $L_m = 1$ consecutive day (must rest the day after working)" or "Werewolf Fenrir can work at most $L_m = 3$ consecutive days," we slide a window of length $L_m + 1$ days across the horizon. Within every contiguous window of $L_m + 1$ days, the guard can work at most $L_m$ days (guaranteeing at least one rest day inside the window):

Sliding-Window Consecutive Work Limit (Window Width L_m + 1) $$ \sum_{k = 0}^{L_m} (\text{day}_{m, \text{start} + k} + \text{night}_{m, \text{start} + k}) \le L_m \quad (\forall \text{start} \in \{0, \dots, T - L_m - 1\}) $$
💡 Why the Sliding-Window Formulation Is Effective
It expresses arbitrary consecutive-day limits $L_m$ using pure linear inequalities without auxiliary state counters or non-linear branching. It also yields a tight LP relaxation, allowing branch-and-bound solvers to converge rapidly.

03Linearizing Logic (Part 1): Rookie Slime's "No Solo Night Duty"

Rookie guards like Pururu the Slime have a supervision rule: "She cannot be assigned to a night shift alone; at least one other colleague must work the same night shift." (This mirrors hospital rostering rules where first-year nurses cannot staff a night ward solo.)

Logically, this is the implication $\text{night}_{\text{pururu}, d} = 1 \implies \sum_{m \neq \text{pururu}} \text{night}_{m, d} \ge 1$. Because all variables are binary, it translates into a single linear inequality:

Linear Inequality for Supervised Night Duty $$ \text{night}_{\text{pururu}, d} - \sum_{m \in M \setminus \{\text{pururu}\}} \text{night}_{m, d} \le 0 \quad (\forall d \in D) $$

When no other guard is assigned to night duty on day $d$ (the sum is $0$), the inequality forces $\text{night}_{\text{pururu}, d} \le 0$. As soon as at least one colleague is assigned (the sum is $1$ or more), $\text{night}_{\text{pururu}, d} \le 1$ allows Pururu to join the shift.

04Linearizing Logic (Part 2): Pairwise Synergies & Conflicts (x_A * x_B)

Guard chemistry plays a central role in building a strong defense line:

  • Synergy Pairs ($\Delta_{A,B} > 0$): Assigning both $A$ and $B$ to the same slot $(d, s)$ grants a $+\Delta_{A,B}$ (+100) teamwork bonus to defense power and morale.
  • Incompatible Pairs ($\Delta_{A,B} < 0$): Assigning both $A$ and $B$ to the same slot triggers a $\Delta_{A,B}$ (-150) conflict penalty.

Written directly, this introduces the quadratic product $x_{A,d,s} \cdot x_{B,d,s}$ of two binary variables, which is non-linear.

Standard Linearization via Auxiliary Binary Variable $\text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} \in \{0, 1\}$ (Fortet / McCormick)

We introduce an auxiliary binary variable $\text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} \in \{0, 1\}$ that equals $1$ if and only if both $A$ and $B$ are assigned to slot $(d, s)$, governed by three linear inequalities:

Three Linear Inequalities Enforcing pair == x_A * x_B $$ \begin{aligned} \text{(a)} \quad & \text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} - x_{A,d,s} \le 0 && (\text{if A is absent }(0)\text{, pair}=0) \\ \text{(b)} \quad & \text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} - x_{B,d,s} \le 0 && (\text{if B is absent }(0)\text{, pair}=0) \\ \text{(c)} \quad & x_{A,d,s} + x_{B,d,s} - \text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} \le 1 && (\text{if both present }(1+1=2)\text{, pair}=1) \end{aligned} $$
💡 Why Both Upper and Lower Bounds Matter Here
For a positive synergy bonus ($\Delta_{A,B} > 0$), upper bounds (a) and (b) alone would suffice because maximization naturally pushes $\text{pair}$ up to $1$. Conversely, for a negative conflict penalty ($\Delta_{A,B} < 0$), the solver tries to set $\text{pair} = 0$ to dodge the penalty; inequality (c) provides the lower bound $\text{pair} \ge x_A + x_B - 1$ that forces $\text{pair} = 1$ whenever both guards share a slot.
💡 Continuous Relaxation of pair and Solver Presolve
Conceptually, $\text{pair}_{A,B,d,s}$ is introduced as a binary decision variable, but once $x_A, x_B \in \{0, 1\}$ are fixed, inequalities (a)–(c) naturally force $\text{pair}$ to a single integer value ($0$ or $1$).
Hence, declaring it as a continuous variable ($0 \le \text{pair} \le 1$) yields identical optimal solutions.
In practice, modern MILP solvers like HiGHS feature aggressive Presolve routines (specifically, implied integer detection) that recognize such structural dependencies automatically and prune redundant branching candidates even if declared binary. Nonetheless, recognizing which variables drive core discrete decisions versus dependent auxiliary terms is an essential modeling discipline.

05Defense Coverage Constraints and Alternative Solutions (No-Good Cuts)

In each slot $(d, s)$, the sum of individual effective defense powers $P_{m,s}$ plus pairwise modifiers must cover the required power $R_{d,s}$ and minimum headcount $N_{d,s}$, while maximizing total castle morale (summed over unordered pairs $\{A, B\} \subseteq M, A < B$ to prevent duplicate counting):

Slot Coverage Constraints and Objective Function $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{Defense Coverage:} && \sum_{m \in M} P_{m,s} \cdot x_{m,d,s} + \sum_{\{A, B\} \subseteq M, A < B} \Delta_{A,B} \cdot \text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} \ge R_{d,s} \\ &\text{Minimum Staff:} && \sum_{m \in M} x_{m,d,s} \ge N_{d,s} \\ &\text{Objective:} && \max \quad 1000 + \sum_{d,s} \left( \sum_{m \in M} \text{morale}_{m,s} \cdot x_{m,d,s} + \sum_{\{A, B\} \subseteq M, A < B} \Delta_{A,B} \cdot \text{pair}_{A,B,d,s} \right) \end{aligned} $$

Enumerating Alternative Rosters with a "No-Good Cut"

In both real-world scheduling and puzzle design, we often want to inspect alternative valid schedules. Given an existing binary solution with active ones S_1 and zeros S_0, adding a single No-Good Cut (Canonical Integer Cut) excludes that exact assignment pattern and finds the next-best (or tied optimal) schedule differing in at least one cell:

Crucially, the cut sets $S_1, S_0$ are constructed strictly from the primary decision variables $x_{m,d,s}$ rather than auxiliary variables like $\text{pair}$, guaranteeing the tightest non-redundant cutting plane. 

// No-Good Cut forbidding the exact previous 0-1 schedule assignment
// Σ_{v ∈ S_1} v - Σ_{u ∈ S_0} u <= |S_1| - 1
m.constraint(
  expr`sum(${activeOnes}) - sum(${activeZeros}) <= ${activeOnes.length - 1}`,
  "forbid_exact_schedule"
);
